new:
This argument is hard to follow, but it seems to be doing something Circular.
It's trying to prove that its printed label is accurate by pointing to evidence that health conscious people buy the product. But how do we know health conscious people buy the product? Because the label is accurate.
Let's look at our two provided rules:
Health conscious consumers buying this cereal → health claims on label true
Health conscious consumers buying a food → health claims on package true
The author is trying to establish that the health claims on the package are true, so he needs to establish that health conscious consumers buy this food.
But he's never established that the people who buy the food are health conscious. He tries to prove that by citing a rule in the last sentence that is essentially the same as the rule stated in the second sentence.

new: Since this has three conditional logic claims (if / only if / if) and has ideas that show up multiple times (squirrels eat / attract birds / protective cover), we would probably be wise to diagram this symbolically. And since we're doing Flaw / Parallel Flaw and we're seeing conditional logic, we can already be 90% sure that the flaw in the argument is an illegal negation or reversal (i.e. the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw). The author is trying to put together two conditionals to arrive at her conclusion. Since "squirrels eating" is the common term in the two conditional premises, it's supposed to be the middle link in the chain. The author thinks she's combining these two premises: No cover → Squirrels eat Squirrels eat → Not many birds If those were actually the two premises, then she would correctly be deriving her conclusion: No cover → Not many birds The problem is the second premise says, Squirrels eat → No cover The word "only if" is the opposite of "if". When we see "if", the idea that goes with that word ends up on the left side of the arrow (the sufficient condition). When we see "only if", the idea that goes with that ends up on the right side (necessary condition).

new: This answer makes two problematic claims. First, it introduces a requirement that patients "focus on other people's troubles," which is not what the argument discusses. The argument is about patients' own relationships, not about focusing on other people's troubles. Second, the claim that psychotherapists "cannot help change" patients' relationships without this focus goes far beyond what the argument needs to assume. The argument needs only the assumption that internal-only treatment is insufficient for healing; it does not need any specific claim about what prevents therapists from changing relationships. This answer mischaracterizes the relational focus the argument describes and imposes a requirement the argument does not demand.

new: This answer claims that patients who change their relationships will "thereby find relief from at least some of their troubles." This is a guarantee: if you change the relationships, healing follows. But the argument does not need this strong a claim. The argument needs only that therapy cannot succeed by addressing internal causes alone; it needs the relational focus to be necessary, not to be sufficient by itself. The argument's conclusion is that therapists must focus on relational change, not that relational change will definitely cure patients. Negate this answer: "some patients who change their relationships will not find relief from any of their troubles." The argument survives this negation perfectly well: even if relational change is not guaranteed to work, it could still be a necessary component of therapy. The argument does not promise success; it identifies a necessary focus area.
